beats.narration: Begin by framing Introduction to Computational Thinking as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds. Consider this worked case: A student defines a problem to find the shortest path in a network, then specifies inputs (graph), outputs (path length), and expected time complexity. On screen, display a split screen: left shows a problem statement box, right shows a flowchart with input/output boxes and a complexity badge. Annotate with 'specification', 'correctness', and 'bounds' labels. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
beats.title: Introduction to Computational Thinking
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a split screen: left shows a problem statement box, right shows a flowchart with input/output boxes and a complexity badge. Annotate with 'specification', 'correctness', and 'bounds' labels.

beats.narration: Now define Algorithm Expression in Pseudo Code precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Specific topics covered include: expression of algorithms in pseudo code and a programming language; functional and imperative programming techniques; control structures; problem solving using recursion; basic searching and sorting; elementary data structures such as lists, trees, and graphs; and correctness, testing and debugging. Consider this worked case: A student writes a pseudo code function for calculating factorial, then translates it into Python code, noting where comments clarify the logic. On screen, show a side-by-side comparison: left is clean pseudo code with indentation, right is Python code with syntax highlighting. Add a checkmark icon next to 'syntax matches logic' and a magnifying glass over the indentation area. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.
beats.title: Algorithm Expression in Pseudo Code
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a side-by-side comparison: left is clean pseudo code with indentation, right is Python code with syntax highlighting. Add a checkmark icon next to 'syntax matches logic' and a magnifying glass over the indentation area.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Functional vs. Imperative Programming operates in a concrete sequence. Dynamic programming records solutions to overlapping subproblems. Consider this worked case: A student compares a recursive factorial function (functional) with a loop-based factorial function (imperative), noting how each handles state differently. On screen, create a Venn diagram: left circle shows 'pure functions, no side effects', right shows 'mutable state, step-by-step updates'. Overlap shows 'both solve the same problem' with a small code snippet in each quadrant. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.
beats.title: Functional vs. Imperative Programming
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Create a Venn diagram: left circle shows 'pure functions, no side effects', right shows 'mutable state, step-by-step updates'. Overlap shows 'both solve the same problem' with a small code snippet in each quadrant.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Control Structures and make the decision criteria explicit. Graphs can be represented with adjacency structures for traversal and path algorithms. Consider this worked case: A student uses a while loop to count down from 10 to 1, updating a counter variable each iteration until the condition fails. On screen, draw a simple flowchart with a decision diamond ('counter > 0?'), a loop back arrow, and an exit path. Highlight the condition check and the update step with distinct colors. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.
beats.title: Control Structures
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Draw a simple flowchart with a decision diamond ('counter > 0?'), a loop back arrow, and an exit path. Highlight the condition check and the update step with distinct colors.

beats.narration: Apply Problem Solving Using Recursion to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results. Consider this worked case: A student implements a recursive function to traverse a directory tree, calling itself for each subdirectory until an empty folder is found. On screen, show a nested tree diagram with the top node labeled 'root', branching into three child nodes, each labeled 'subproblem', and the leaves labeled 'base case'. Add arrows showing the call stack unwinding. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: Problem Solving Using Recursion
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a nested tree diagram with the top node labeled 'root', branching into three child nodes, each labeled 'subproblem', and the leaves labeled 'base case'. Add arrows showing the call stack unwinding.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Basic Searching and Sorting, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. OpenDSA presents data structures and algorithms through executable visualizations and exercises. Consider this worked case: A student sorts a list of student IDs alphabetically using bubble sort, then uses binary search to find a specific ID in the sorted list. On screen, display two columns: left shows an unsorted list transforming into a sorted list with swap arrows, right shows a sorted list with a pointer highlighting the target value and a 'found' badge. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
beats.title: Basic Searching and Sorting
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display two columns: left shows an unsorted list transforming into a sorted list with swap arrows, right shows a sorted list with a pointer highlighting the target value and a 'found' badge.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Elementary Data Structures: Lists, Trees, Graphs with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based operations. Consider this worked case: A student uses a list to track daily expenses, a tree to organize file folders, and a graph to map city bus routes with stops as vertices and routes as edges. On screen, present three icons: a horizontal list with numbered slots, a pyramid-shaped tree with parent-child links, and a network of dots connected by lines. Label each with its primary use case. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Elementary Data Structures: Lists, Trees, Graphs
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Present three icons: a horizontal list with numbered slots, a pyramid-shaped tree with parent-child links, and a network of dots connected by lines. Label each with its primary use case.

beats.narration: Use Correctness, Testing, and Debugging to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. A disciplined solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and then analyzes time and space. Consider this worked case: A student tests a sorting algorithm with empty lists, single elements, and duplicates, then uses a debugger to step through a loop to find an off-by-one error. On screen, show a checklist graphic: 'test empty input', 'test edge case', 'trace loop variable', 'fix error'. Each item has a toggle switch that flips from red to green as the student checks them off. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Correctness, Testing, and Debugging
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a checklist graphic: 'test empty input', 'test edge case', 'trace loop variable', 'fix error'. Each item has a toggle switch that flips from red to green as the student checks them off.

beats.narration: Connect Data Structure Representation and Invariants to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Representation choices and invariants determine which operations are efficient and which errors are possible. Consider this worked case: A student chooses an adjacency list over an adjacency matrix for a sparse graph, noting that the invariant 'each edge appears exactly once' keeps memory usage low. On screen, display two grid layouts: left shows a dense matrix with many empty cells, right shows a sparse adjacency list with short chains. Add a warning icon over the matrix and a checkmark over the list, labeled 'sparse graph invariant'. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Data Structure Representation and Invariants
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display two grid layouts: left shows a dense matrix with many empty cells, right shows a sparse adjacency list with short chains. Add a warning icon over the matrix and a checkmark over the list, labeled 'sparse graph invariant'.

beats.narration: Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Assignments (both in class and for homework) requiring a pseudo code solution and an implementation are an integral part of the course. Consider this worked case: A student reviews a checklist: 'define I/O', 'state loop invariant', 'analyze recurrence', 'verify base case', then proceeds to code the divide-and-conquer algorithm. On screen, show a clean checklist graphic with four boxes: 'specification', 'correctness proof', 'resource bounds', 'implementation'. Each box has a progress bar that fills as the student completes the step, ending with a 'ready to code' badge. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.

sources.excerpt: This course serves as an introduction to computational thinking using a problem-centered approach. Specific topics covered include: expression of algorithms in pseudo code and a programming language; functional and imperative programming techniques; control structures; problem solving using recursion; basic searching and sorting; elementary data structures such as lists, trees, and graphs; and correctness, testing and debugging. sources.author: MIT OpenCourseWare
sources.excerpt: Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds. Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size. A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination. Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results. Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms. Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions. Dynamic programming records solutions to overlapping subproblems. Core methods include sorting, hashing, trees, graphs, shortest paths, and dynamic programming. A disciplined solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and then analyzes time and space.
sources.title: MIT OpenCourseWare Introduction to Algorithms

sources.author: OpenDSA Project
sources.excerpt: OpenDSA presents data structures and algorithms through executable visualizations and exercises. Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based operations. Stacks use last-in, first-out access, while queues use first-in, first-out access. Trees represent hierarchical relationships and support recursive traversals. Hash tables map keys to locations and require a collision strategy. Graphs can be represented with adjacency structures for traversal and path algorithms. Automata and formal languages describe machines, accepted strings, and computational limits. Representation choices and invariants determine which operations are efficient and which errors are possible.
